title: Indexing jsonb, building JSON responses in SQL, when a real column wins
summary: GIN serves containment and jsonpath matches; ranges and sorting on one key need a B-tree on the exact expression the query writes. json keeps the key order you build, jsonb normalizes it. A key that every row has and every query uses wants to be a real, typed, constrained column.

examples.title: GIN for @? and a B-tree expression index for ranges and ORDER BY ... LIMIT

annotations.note: Priority 1 is on 1 % of the tickets, the kvkk label on 2 %: selective conditions, the case where an index pays off.
jsonb_path_ops, the smaller GIN operator class from the GIN lesson: it serves @>, @? and @@, but not the key-existence operators.

A B-tree on an expression. Anything that isn't a plain column or a function call needs its own parentheses, hence the doubled ones. The cast makes it an index of integers, so ranges and sorting compare numbers, not text.
The docs: a new expression index gets statistics only after ANALYZE. Until then the planner has no idea how common priority 1 is and falls back to default estimates.
The jsonpath filter is answered from the GIN index. The plan prints the path in canonical form ($."labels"[*]?(@ == "kvkk")): a jsonpath value is stored parsed, like jsonb.
The 200 priority-1 tickets come from tickets_priority. GIN couldn't help here: <= isn't one of its jsonb operators.

An Index Scan in index order feeds the LIMIT directly: no Sort, and the first five entries read are the answer. For a deterministic top five, add a tie-breaker and index (((doc ->> 'priority')::int), id).

(doc -> 'priority')::int casts jsonb to int (allowed since PG 11) and gives the same numbers, but the planner matches expressions, not meanings: Seq Scan. Keep the indexed expression in one place, such as a view, or promote the key to a column (example 3).

examples.title: Building JSON responses: json vs jsonb key order, whole rows, timestamps, big ids

annotations.note: json_build_object returns json: keys in call order, printed as "key" : value with spaces around the colon. jsonb_build_object returns jsonb: keys stored shorter first (id, code, owner, title) and printed in jsonb's canonical "key": value form. Both are valid JSON; choose json when a client or a snapshot test depends on key order. Turkish text goes out as UTF-8, not as \u escapes.

to_jsonb(row) names keys after columns, so renaming a column renames an API field. - 'id' drops a key; jsonb_strip_nulls drops REQ-2's null owner. For public APIs list the fields explicitly: with to_jsonb, a column added later, say password_hash, would leak.
timestamptz becomes an ISO 8601 string in the session time zone, "2026-11-13T09:00:00+03:00": what JavaScript's Date and Go's time.Time (RFC 3339) parse.

9007199254740993 is exact in jsonb, whose numbers are numeric. A browser's JSON.parse returns 9007199254740992: JavaScript numbers are doubles, exact only up to 2^53 - 1. Send bigint ids as strings, or keep them below that limit.
The subquery-per-list shape from the aggregation lesson: each list is aggregated on its own, and coalesce turns "no tests" into [] instead of NULL.

examples.title: Promoting a key to a STORED generated column with NOT NULL and a foreign key

annotations.note: customer_id and total are in every order; gift_note and coupon only in some. That split is the design question of this lesson.

A STORED generated column computes its value on every write of doc and stores it: a real int column that can be NOT NULL, carry a foreign key and be indexed. doc stays the single source of truth, and the column can never disagree with it. Adding a stored generated column rewrites the table, so on a big table plan it like any rewriting migration.
PostgreSQL 18 makes a generated column VIRTUAL unless you say STORED, and a virtual column can't be indexed or carry a foreign key (both fail with SQLSTATE 0A000). Here STORED is not optional.
The join uses a typed, indexed, constrained column; total still comes out of the document. If every report sums totals, total is the next key to promote.
What remains in the document is genuinely optional data: notes and coupons that vary per order.

SQLSTATE 23503: the foreign key runs on write. A missing customer_id would fail NOT NULL (23502) and a non-numeric one the cast (22P02), also at INSERT time. jsonb alone would have accepted all three.

use_cases: GIN (jsonb_path_ops): filtering event payloads or product attributes by varying keys with @> or jsonpath
B-tree expression index: one hot key used for ranges, sorting or top-N, while the rest stays in the document
JSON built in SQL: API responses with nested lists, CSV-free exports, snapshots for an audit log
STORED generated columns: promoting stable keys of ingested documents (customer, type, created time) to typed, constrained, indexed columns
strengths: One GIN index serves containment and jsonpath filters on any key, without an index per attribute
Expression indexes give one key B-tree powers (ranges, ORDER BY ... LIMIT) and planner statistics, without changing the table
SQL-built JSON is escaped correctly and arrives in one round trip; the Go or TS layer can pass it through
A generated column turns a document field into a real column (types, NOT NULL, foreign keys, statistics) while the document stays the source
weaknesses: GIN can't do ranges or ordering, and an expression index serves only the exact expression it was built on
Statistics on keys inside a document exist only for indexed or declared expressions; everything else is estimated with defaults
json and jsonb render keys differently, and to_jsonb(row) couples API field names to column names
Promotion costs a table rewrite for a stored generated column, and every promoted key is one more place a schema change must reach

pitfalls.title: Writing the expression differently from the index
pitfalls.detail: (doc -> 'k')::int and (doc ->> 'k')::int mean the same thing, but only the indexed spelling uses the index. Put the expression in one view or function, or make it a column.

pitfalls.title: A generated column without STORED in PostgreSQL 18
pitfalls.detail: Since PG 18 the default is VIRTUAL, computed on read, and a virtual column can't have an index or a foreign key. Say STORED when the column exists to be indexed or referenced.
pitfalls.bad: ADD COLUMN customer_id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((doc ->> 'customer_id')::int)
pitfalls.good: ADD COLUMN customer_id int GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((doc ->> 'customer_id')::int) STORED

pitfalls.title: bigint ids as JSON numbers for JavaScript clients
pitfalls.detail: Ids above 2^53 - 1 lose precision in JSON.parse without any error. Send them as strings (t.id::text), or use ids that stay below the limit.

pitfalls.title: to_jsonb(row) as a public API
pitfalls.detail: Every column, including ones added later, becomes a field. Build the object from an explicit list of keys.
pitfalls.good: SELECT jsonb_build_object('id', u.id::text, 'name', u.name) FROM users u

pitfalls.title: Expecting jsonb to keep the key order you built
pitfalls.detail: jsonb stores keys shorter-first and then bytewise, so id comes before code whatever you wrote. Use the json variants (json_build_object, json_agg) when order matters to a consumer.

quiz.q: There is a GIN index on `doc` (jsonb_path_ops). Which condition can it serve?
quiz.why: jsonb_path_ops supports @>, @? and @@. Ranges are B-tree work, and key existence needs the default jsonb_ops class.

quiz.q: The index is on `((doc ->> 'priority')::int)`. Does `WHERE (doc -> 'priority')::int = 1` use it?
options: No, the planner matches the indexed expression, not its meaning
quiz.why: Index matching is syntactic on the expression tree; -> plus a jsonb-to-int cast is a different expression.
jsonb stores keys shorter first; the third form is what json_build_object would print.

quiz.q: Every order has a customer_id that reports join on and that must reference customers. Where should it live?
options: In the jsonb document, with a GIN index
In a column (or a STORED generated column) with NOT NULL and a foreign key
In a VIRTUAL generated column with a foreign key
quiz.why: Only a stored column can be NOT NULL, indexed and referenced by a foreign key; PG 18 rejects foreign keys and indexes on virtual generated columns.

further_reading.title: PostgreSQL docs: CREATE STATISTICS (statistics on a single expression)

body:
## Concept

Three decisions come with every `jsonb` column.

**How to index it.** The GIN lesson covered the whole-document index: `jsonb_ops` (all
keys and values, serves `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&`, `@?`, `@@`) and the smaller
`jsonb_path_ops` (`@>`, `@?`, `@@`). GIN finds documents that *contain* something. It
can't answer ranges or sorting, so a key used with `<`, `BETWEEN` or `ORDER BY` needs a
**B-tree expression index** on exactly the expression the query writes, such as
`((doc ->> 'priority')::int)`. An expression index also gives the planner statistics
for that expression after `ANALYZE`; `CREATE STATISTICS ... ON (expression)` (PG 14)
gives the statistics without the index.

**How to build JSON for clients.** `json_build_object`/`jsonb_build_object`, `to_jsonb`
on a row, and the aggregates from the aggregation lesson produce the response document
in SQL. `json` output keeps your key order; `jsonb` output is canonical: keys shorter
first, one space after the colon. Dates become ISO 8601 strings, numbers stay exact
numerics, which JavaScript can't always represent.

**When a column wins.** If every row has the key and queries filter, join, sort or
aggregate on it, or it must be `NOT NULL`, unique or a foreign key, it should be a
column. A `STORED` generated column extracts it from the document on every write, so
ingested payloads stay intact and the column can't drift from them.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS/TS:** `JSON.parse` turns every number into a double. Ids above
  `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1) come back rounded, without an error, so bigint ids
  travel as strings. On the way in, a jsonb column is `unknown` until zod has checked it;
  a promoted column is a type the database already checked.
- **Go:** `encoding/json` decodes a JSON number into `float64` when the target is `any`,
  with the same precision problem; a struct field of type `int64`, or the `,string` tag
  option, keeps it exact. pgx can scan a SQL-built JSON column straight into
  `json.RawMessage` and the handler can write it out unchanged.
- **Java:** a jsonb column is like a `Map<String, Object>` field in an entity: flexible,
  and invisible to every constraint and index you'd put on a real field. Promoting a key
  is the same refactoring as replacing a map entry with a typed field.
- **Document databases:** there you index paths inside documents. Postgres gives you
  that (GIN, expression indexes) and also lets you move a hot path into a typed,
  constrained column without leaving the table.

## How it works

The planner considers an expression index when the query contains the indexed
expression itself; an equivalent spelling doesn't count, as the last plan of example 1
shows: `(doc -> 'priority')::int` missed the index that `(doc ->> 'priority')::int` used.
In return, the docs point out, the search is as fast as on a plain column, because the
expression's values are stored in the index and not recomputed (they are computed on
every insert and non-HOT update instead). It also explains why the
generated column is the robust solution: every query writes `customer_id`, and there is
nothing to spell differently.

Without statistics on an expression, the planner falls back to fixed guesses. The
`CREATE STATISTICS` docs give 0.5 % selectivity for equality and range conditions in
that case. A key whose values are very skewed (one tenant with half the rows) is
exactly where that guess goes wrong, and where an expression index or a column, both of
which `ANALYZE` measures, fixes the plans.

## Design notes

Structured where it's stable, JSON where it isn't. Walk each key of a document through
three questions: does every row have it, do queries filter, join, sort or aggregate on
it, and does it need a constraint? Any yes makes it a candidate column. What stays in
the document is the long tail: optional attributes, integration-specific fields, the raw
payload kept for replay.

When the document is the record (an order received from a shop, a webhook you must be
able to replay), promote with a `STORED` generated column and leave the document
untouched. When the application owns the data, make it an ordinary column, backfill it,
and remove the key from the document, so there is one source of truth.

For responses, let SQL build the shape when the response is a straightforward
projection of the data: one round trip, correct escaping, and no N+1 queries. Choose
`json` when key order is part of the contract, list keys explicitly instead of
`to_jsonb(row)` for anything public, and send bigint ids as strings to JavaScript
clients.

files.examples/02_responses.sql:
SET TimeZone = 'Europe/Istanbul';

CREATE TABLE requirements (
  id         bigint      PRIMARY KEY,
  code       text        NOT NULL,
  title      text        NOT NULL,
  owner      text,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE test_cases (
  id             bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  requirement_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES requirements,
  status         text   NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO requirements VALUES
  (1, 'REQ-1', 'Giriş ekranı', 'Zeynep', '2026-11-13 09:00+03'),
  (2, 'REQ-2', 'Dışa aktarım', NULL,     '2026-11-13 10:30+03');
INSERT INTO test_cases VALUES
  (9007199254740993, 1, 'passed'), (11, 1, 'failed');

-- json keeps the keys in the order you wrote them; jsonb sorts them
-- (shorter first) and prints its own canonical spacing.
SELECT json_build_object('code', code, 'title', title, 'owner', owner, 'id', id)
         AS as_json,
       jsonb_build_object('code', code, 'title', title, 'owner', owner, 'id', id)
         AS as_jsonb
FROM requirements
WHERE id = 1;

-- A whole row: keys come from column names; - removes what the client
-- shouldn't get, jsonb_strip_nulls the fields that are null.
SELECT jsonb_strip_nulls(to_jsonb(r) - 'id') AS body
FROM requirements AS r
ORDER BY r.id;

-- One response document per requirement. timestamptz becomes ISO 8601 in
-- the session time zone; ids also go out as strings for JavaScript.
SELECT jsonb_build_object(
         'code', r.code,
         'created_at', r.created_at,
         'tests', (SELECT coalesce(jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
                                     'id', t.id, 'id_str', t.id::text,
                                     'status', t.status) ORDER BY t.id), '[]')
                   FROM test_cases AS t
                   WHERE t.requirement_id = r.id)) AS body
FROM requirements AS r
ORDER BY r.id;
